# Tooling index — every `tools/`, `mechanisms/scripts/` script in `agentic-practices-bs`

One row per tool, extracted from each script's own header text, so a cold agent can
find existing tooling instead of rebuilding it or doing the job by hand. **This is a
projection, not a second copy** — it is regenerated from the source files and a stale
copy fails the commit, so it cannot drift the way a hand-written list would.

**Scope is this repo only.** Each repo carries its own index, generated from its own
`tools/`, `mechanisms/scripts/`, so nothing here depends on what is checked out next door. The sibling repos
have their own `docs/TOOLS-index.md`; if you need theirs, read it there.

**The scan is recursive**, and a tool in a subdirectory is named by its path under
`tools/`, `mechanisms/scripts/` (`capture-analysis/deep.py`). It was top-level-only until 2026-08-10, which
silently omitted ten tools across the four repos — including five analyzers that were
being cited as the example of tooling nobody can find.

**`.py`, `.ps1`, and `.sh`** are catalogued. PowerShell was added 2026-08-11; `.py`-only
was never a decision, and it hid the firmware repo's entire bench workflow (build, flash,
OTA push/deliver, the flash gate) from the one page meant to surface it. `.sh` was added
2026-08-16 for the same reason one step further: `tools/archive-elf.sh` is called by the
flash gate and OTA push SPECIFICALLY because it propagates a real exit code where the
`.ps1` variant always exits 0 — i.e. the script that actually gates flashing was invisible
to this index. Neither `.ps1` nor `.sh` has a docstring, so their description comes from
the leading header comment — `<# … #>` (PowerShell only) or a run of `#` lines (both) —
which is what these scripts already wrote; none was edited to be listed. The self-naming
prefix (`build-boards.ps1 --`, `archive-elf.sh —`) is stripped since the row names the
file anyway. `tags:` and `fail:` are read from that same header, so either can opt into
them; the ones that have not read `UNASSESSED`, which is an answer rather than a gap.

`tags:` is **what you would search for before knowing the tool existed** — the
condition you are in, not what the script does. Grep this file for your situation, not
for a filename. Tags sit on the tool's own line so a hit always names its tool.
`UNASSESSED` means nobody could honestly name search terms; it is a real answer, and
better than an invented tag that makes a tool look considered when nobody looked.

`fail:` answers one narrow question — **if you do this task the obvious way and the**
**obvious way is wrong, do you find out?** It is not an estimate of what the tool saves.
`loud` = it errors, returns nothing, or visibly breaks, so you notice and go looking.
`silent` = the obvious way returns a plausible *wrong* answer and you proceed on it.
`silent-artifact` = worse, that wrong result gets committed and someone else inherits it.
Every `silent` states the specific wrong answer you would get; a grade that cannot name
one is refused by the generator rather than published.

`born:` is the subject of the commit that CREATED the tool, extracted — never written.
In this codebase tools are born from incidents, so the birth certificate is usually the
cost of not using it, stated by whoever had just paid it. Personal names and one
project-specific referent are rewritten by a fixed substitution table so the line stays
portable; everything else is the commit subject verbatim.

`no caller` means no *other* tracked file **in this repo** mentions the script: a
manual-run or one-shot tool, not a dead one — and, since the scan stops at this repo's
edge, possibly one whose only caller lives in a sibling. They are listed for the same
reason as the rest — being hand-invoked is precisely what makes a tool easy to forget,
which is also why an unwired tool needs its tags more than a wired one, not less.

**14 tools; 2 with no in-repo caller; 14 UNASSESSED tags. fail: 0 loud, 0 silent, 0 silent-artifact.**
